chunks: My father narrated to us, may God be pleased with him, saying: Ali ibn al-Husayn al-Sa'd Abadi narrated to us, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah al-Barqi, from Ali ibn Ma'bad, from al-Husayn ibn Khalid, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him: 'For how many people does the offering of a camel suffice?' He said: 'For one person.' I said: 'And the cow?' He said: 'It suffices for five, if they all eat at one table.' I said: 'Why has it become that the camel suffices for only one, while the cow suffices for five?'

He said: 'Because the camel lacked the reason (cause) that was present in the cow. Indeed, those who ordered the people of Moses (peace be upon him) to worship the calf were five persons, and they were a family who ate at one table. They were: Azinooh, his brother Mibdhawi, his cousin, his daughter, and his wife. And they were the ones who slaughtered the cow that God, the Exalted, commanded to be slaughtered.'

The compiler of this book, may God be pleased with him, said: 'This hadith came thus, so I included it because of the mention of five within it. However, my legal opinion regarding the camel is that it suffices for seven, and likewise the cow suffices for seven separate individuals. These narrations are not contradictory, because what suffices for seven also suffices for one, and suffices for five as well. And in this hadith there is no statement that the camel suffies for only one, nor that the cow suffices for only five.'

key_terms.الْبَدَنَةُ: A mature female camel used for sacrifice
key_terms.الْعِلَّةُ: The underlying reason or cause (in legal context)

ai.seo_question: How many people can a single camel or cow sacrifice suffice for in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq records this narration from Imam al-Rida (AS), linking the Islamic ruling of Qurbani to the specific historical incident of the Israelites who slaughtered the Cow (Surah Al-Baqarah) as a form of repentance. The compiler clarifies that the numbers one, five, and seven are not mutually exclusive limits but rather overlapping sufficiencies, demonstrating the flexibility (tawassu') in Shia fiqh regarding sacrificial offerings.
